content: 1. A photomicrograph of a vaginal smear specimen shows two epithelial cells: one normal and one covered with bacteria, giving it a rough, stippled appearance known as a clue cell. Clue cells are epithelial cells with bacteria adhered to their surface, obscuring their borders and imparting a stippled appearance. The presence of clue cells is indicative of bacterial vaginosis. 2. Gardnerella vaginalis, formerly known as Haemophilus vaginalis or Corynebacterium vaginalis, is a bacterium that helps regulate vaginal pH, maintaining it in a low range to inhibit the growth of potentially pathogenic organisms. 3. A photomicrograph reveals bacteria adhering to vaginal epithelial cells, forming clue cells. These cells have bacteria on their surface, obscuring their borders and giving them a stippled appearance, which is a hallmark of bacterial vaginosis. 4. A Gram-stained photomicrograph of a vaginal specimen at 63x magnification shows squamous epithelial cells, polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs or white blood cells), and numerous Gram-positive bacilli. Vaginal specimens are reviewed for various reasons, including Pap tests and tests for sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) like human papillomavirus (HPV) and Chlamydia trachomatis. 5. A photomicrograph of Chlamydia trachomatis from a urethral scrape shows intracellular inclusion bodies in McCoy cell monolayers, representing the replication phase of the bacterium. Chlamydia, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection. 6. A close-up image of a patient's left eye with the upper lid retracted reveals inflamed conjunctival membranes due to inclusion conjunctivitis, a type of conjunctival inflammation caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. This condition, also known as chlamydial conjunctivitis, is more common in newborns. 7. A photomicrograph of HeLa cells infected with Type-A Chlamydia trachomatis shows intracellular inclusion bodies. HeLa cells can be used to culture Chlamydia trachomatis. 8. Genital herpes is a sexually transmitted disease caused by herpes simplex viruses type 1 (HSV-1) or type 2 (HSV-2). Most genital herpes cases are caused by HSV-2. Symptoms, when present, typically appear as one or more blisters on or around the genitals or rectum. These blisters break, leaving tender ulcers that may take two to four weeks to heal during the first outbreak. 9. A male patient presented with maculopapular lesions on the distal penile shaft, initially suspected to be syphilis but later diagnosed as a Herpesviridae infection through differential diagnosis. 10. A neonate displayed maculopapular lesions on the foot due to congenital herpes simplex virus infection, known as herpes simplex neonatorum. Neonatal herpes can cause potentially fatal infections in babies, and cesarean delivery is often performed if the mother has active genital herpes at the time of delivery. 11. A 7-year-old child with a history of recurrent herpes labialis presented with a periocular herpes simplex vesicular outbreak. Another patient presented with vesiculopapular herpes simplex lesions on the anterior thigh, which had not yet ruptured. 12. Gonorrhea, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is a sexually transmitted infection that can cause localized infections in the genital tract or disseminated infections affecting various organs. If left untreated, the bacteria can enter the bloodstream and spread throughout the body. 13. A patient presented with a gonococcal lesion on the distal fingertip, while another had a gonococcal infection involving the cervix. Disseminated gonococcal infections can cause cutaneous lesions, such as those observed on the hand, ankle, or calf. 14. Gonococcal conjunctivitis, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, can lead to partial blindness if untreated. Neonates are at risk of acquiring this infection during delivery if the mother is infected. 15. A patient with gonorrhea presented with penile discharge and paraphimosis. Specimen collection for gonorrhea diagnosis involves expressing pus from the urethra and using a sterile swab for testing. 16. Pubic lice infestation, caused by Phthirus pubis, involves parasitic insects that feed on human blood. Lice infestations are spread through close person-to-person contact and are treated with over-the-counter or prescription medications. Only body lice are known to spread disease.
